power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Mental health is shaped by multiple factors, including the built environment.
As urbanisation increases, urban living has been associated with higher rates of depression, anxiety and psychosis, although the evidence remains predominantly associative.

Here, we synthesise epidemiological, neuroimaging and environmental research into a six-domain framework for understanding how built-environment qualities may relate to mental health risk and resilience.
The domains comprise Safety and Accessibility, Cognitive Load and Environmental Complexity, Multisensory Integration, Emotional Valence, Social Connection, and Naturalness and Biophilia.
We link these domains to neural, physiological, cognitive, emotional and social pathways, and outline methods for testing them across environmental, experiential and neurobiological levels.
The framework provides a structure for developing more precise and testable hypotheses about how specific characteristics of the built environment may influence mental health and resilience.

Mental health is closely associated with overall health, daily functioning and quality of life. 1 Today, more than 50% of the world's population lives in cities, a figure projected to reach approximately 70% by 2050. 2, 3 Alongside rapid urbanisation, mental health conditions are increasing worldwide, 4 and urban living has been associated with a higher prevalence of depression, anxiety, psychosis and schizophrenia. 5, 6 The surrounding environment shapes behaviour, stress and mental health across the lifespan. 7 City living has also been linked to differences in brain structure and function, particularly in systems involved in stress regulation. 8, 9 At the same time, cities offer important benefits, including access to education, healthcare, employment, culture and diversity. 10 Features including greenspace and biophilic design may reduce stress and support mental health and wellbeing, 9, 11 while other environmental characteristics have been associated with cognitive functioning and reduced psychiatric risk. 12, 13 The central question is therefore which features of urban environments contribute to risk or resilience, for whom, and through which mechanisms. 14 Understanding these relationships requires consideration of biological, psychological, behavioural and social pathways, together with individual susceptibility and selection. 15 Vulnerability may vary through gene × environment interaction, 16 while individuals may select environments that correspond with partly genetically influenced characteristics, a process described as selective migration. 17, 18 Individuals with higher genetic risk for psychiatric disorders may, for example, be more likely to migrate to urban areas. 19 Environmental exposure must therefore be distinguished from susceptibility, selection and adaptation when interpreting associations between urban environments and mental health.

text.text: Building on evidence from epidemiology, neuroscience, environmental psychology and built-environment research, this article proposes a six-domain neurobiological framework for examining how specific environmental qualities may relate to mental health risk and resilience.

The framework connects environmental features with subjective experience and candidate neural, physiological, cognitive, emotional, behavioural and social pathways, while recognising that much of the current evidence remains associative.

We first review evidence linking urban and natural environments with mental health and brain-related outcomes, then introduce the six domains and their proposed mechanisms, before considering methodological approaches needed to test the framework.
The aim is to support more precise, testable hypotheses about how specific features of the built environment may influence mental health.

A substantial body of evidence suggests that urban living is associated with elevated risk for several psychiatric conditions. 6 In a review combining an ecological analysis across 191 countries with a synthesis of meta-analytic studies, van der Wal et al. 6 found a positive, non-linear relationship between urbanicity and the prevalence of common mental disorders, most pronounced for anxiety, and identified ambient (e.g. air pollution, noise), physical (e.g. housing, urban design, green space), and social (e.g. socioeconomic deprivation, crime, social cohesion) features associated with risk that differed by diagnosis.

text.text: A more recent narrative review of 48 studies similarly found that natural elements around the home, particularly parks and trees, were most consistently associated with better mental and brain health, whereas generic green-space measures often showed no association, and built elements such as street networks, density and public transport showed mixed effects, reflecting trade-offs between accessibility and exposure to noise and pollution. 20 Urbanicity should therefore not be treated as a single exposure.

text.text: Associations with mental health likely reflect multiple co-occurring conditions, including air and noise pollution, housing quality, density, and differential access to restorative green and blue space, rather than a single undifferentiated "urban" effect.
These exposures are also correlated with broader socioeconomic and institutional conditions that may confound or modify observed relationships.

Gene-environment correlation may further contribute: polygenic risk for several psychiatric disorders has been associated with living in, and moving to, more densely populated areas. 19 Depression, the most prevalent mental disorder globally, 4 has also been reported more frequently among urban than rural populations, with similar patterns for generalised anxiety disorder and psychosis. 5, 21 Neuroimaging research further suggests that urban exposure may be associated with variation in neural systems involved in stress processing and emotion regulation.

text.text: Accelerated brain ageing was associated with reduced green-space access, higher PM2.5 emissions, non-methane volatile organic pollutants, extreme precipitation and higher maximum temperature, alongside lower socioeconomic equality, human capital, gender equality, civil participation, political representation, rule of law, basic welfare and access to justice.

Physical exposures were more strongly related to structural ageing, whereas social and political exposures were more closely associated with functional ageing; importantly, combined exposome models substantially outperformed isolated exposures, indicating cumulative rather than single-factor effects.
Much of this literature nevertheless remains limited in its ability to establish causality.

Large-scale and longitudinal studies such as Legaz et al., 23 Engemann et al., 12 and Quinones et al., 24 the latter linking neighbourhood-level air pollutants, population density and land-use composition to two-year changes in whole-brain structure in older adults, therefore provide a stronger basis for examining how sustained environmental exposure may shape brain and mental health over time, although socioeconomic conditions and access to care remain difficult to fully disentangle.

text.text: Several strategies have been used to strengthen causal inference.

Prospective and registry-based longitudinal designs, such as those described above, establish the temporal order of exposure and outcome, although they remain vulnerable to residential selection and unmeasured confounding.

Family-based designs address confounding shared within families: in a nationwide Swedish cohort of 2.4 million individuals, associations between population density or neighbourhood deprivation and schizophrenia were explained by familial factors when siblings were compared. 25 Genetic approaches indicate that selection may also contribute, as people with higher genetic risk for schizophrenia are more likely to live in densely populated areas, and Mendelian randomisation analyses suggest that this genetic liability may itself influence where people live. 26 Mendelian randomisation is more difficult to apply to the built environment directly, because residential exposures are not themselves genetically determined; its main value in this context is in testing reverse causation and selection, and in examining intermediate traits.

text.text: Randomised and quasi-experimental changes in environment provide the strongest designs: in the Moving to Opportunity experiment, offering families vouchers to move to lower-poverty neighbourhoods improved adults' subjective wellbeing over 10-15 years. 27 Within-person studies that follow the same individuals before and after environmental change, and natural experiments arising from urban regeneration or greening, are therefore likely to be central to establishing causal pathways for specific urban exposures (Fig. 1).

text.text: Within this broader context, natural environments may represent an important source of resilience.

A growing body of research links nature exposure to mental health and resilience. 9, 11, 12, 22, [28] [29] [30] In a nationwide Danish cohort, greater residential greenspace exposure during childhood was associated with a lower risk of developing a range of psychiatric disorders from adolescence into adulthood, after adjustment for urbanisation, parental and municipal socioeconomic factors, parental history of mental illness, and parental age. 12 Similar effects have been attributed to bluespace, 31 although greenspace and bluespace commonly co-occur with lower pollution and noise, greater opportunities for physical activity, safer neighbourhoods, and greater socioeconomic resources, making causal attribution difficult.

text.text: The benefits of greenspace are not confined to childhood.

In adulthood, proximity to greenspace has been associated with reduced antidepressant use after adjustment for individual and neighbourhood socioeconomic and urban-context covariates. 30 Potential pathways include stress reduction, attentional restoration, physical activity, social connection, immune function, and neuroendocrine regulation. 10, 32 Neuroimaging findings point in a similar direction.

text.text: Proximity to forest coverage has been positively associated with structural amygdala integrity in older adults, 9 while exclusive rural versus urban upbringing has been associated with differences in left hippocampal formation volume linked to spatial processing. 22 Using a hybrid ecological momentary assessment-neuroimaging design, Tost et al. 33 found that greater green-related affective benefit was related to lower prefrontal activity during negative-emotion processing, suggesting that urban green space exposure may compensate for reduced neural regulatory capacity.

text.text: More broadly, natural features integrated into architecture, design, and infrastructure may help buffer urban stressors. 11 Lower depression prevalence has been associated with urban environments characterised by both greenspace and high-quality housing, 34 while long-term urban greenness has been linked to slower biological and epigenetic ageing. 28, 35 Sky view in the residential environment has also been associated with prefrontal grey matter in children. 36 These findings support further examination of the amount, quality, connectivity, and proximity of green space required to produce meaningful effects, as well as variation across age, socioeconomic conditions, and neurocognitive profiles.

text.text: One potential pathway linking repeated environmental exposure to mental health is stress regulation.

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a central brain-body stress-response system, 37 supporting adaptive responses to acute stress through the release of corticotropin-releasing hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol. 38 Prolonged or repeated activation can, however, contribute to allostatic load and adverse effects across the brain and body, [39] [40] [41] including cardiovascular and immune dysfunction, slower wound healing and greater vulnerability to stress-related illness. 42, 43 Several features of the built environment may contribute to such stress-related pathways.

text.text: Higher traffic volumes have been associated with more depressive symptoms, and greater traffic-noise exposure with poorer mental health. 46, 47 Noise may activate the sympathetic nervous system and elevate brain-body stress responses, 48, 49 while persistent organic and heavy-metal pollutants are being investigated in relation to psychiatric disorders, 50 and traffic-related air pollution has been linked to psychiatric risk, potentially through neuroinflammatory pathways. 51 Urban form may also influence mental health through behaviour and sensory exposure.

text.text: Car-oriented environments can constrain physical activity, an important determinant of mental health, 52, 53 while pavement width and city walkability are associated with residents' physical activity. 54 High-rise environments may also influence affect: high-rise buildings have been perceived as less friendly and open, with participants reporting feeling less happy and less in control than in low-rise environments. 55 High-rise development may additionally reduce access to natural daylight, which is relevant to mental health and wellbeing. 56 Insufficient daytime light combined with excessive artificial light at night can disrupt circadian rhythms and sleep, with consequences for mood and mental health. 57, 58 Allostatic interoceptive overload provides one possible account of how cumulative urban exposures may become biologically embedded. 59, 60 When repeated environmental demands such as pollution, noise, deprivation, social adversity or perceived threat exceed an individual's regulatory capacity, stress responses may become persistently elevated and increasingly poorly matched to bodily needs.

text.text: Altered regulation across the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala and connected brain-body systems may then contribute to autonomic, HPA-axis, metabolic, inflammatory and immune dysregulation, potentially increasing vulnerability to anxiety, depression and other brain disorders.
Importantly, people do not ordinarily experience environmental characteristics as isolated variables.

Rather, spatial, sensory, social, and emotional features are integrated into higher-order subjective experiences that may mediate how environments influence behaviour and mental health. 61 Research on architectural experience has identified coherence, fascination, and hominess as three important experiential dimensions: coherence reflects the ease with which a setting can be organised and understood, fascination its capacity to attract interest and attention, and hominess the extent to which it evokes warmth, comfort, or personal connection. 62, 63

text.text: Drawing on existing evidence from neuroscience, psychology, and physiology, we identify six domains of neuroenvironmental interaction (Table 1).
text.formatted: Drawing on existing evidence from neuroscience, psychology, and physiology, we identify six domains of neuroenvironmental interaction (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Each represents a distinct but interrelated pathway through which environmental characteristics are perceived and translated into responses relevant to mental health, cognitive performance, and wellbeing.

Together, the domains capture the relationship between external environmental affordances and internal experiential processes, reflecting continuous interplay between perception, cognition, emotion, and context. 29, [64] [65] [66] The domains were identified through a narrative synthesis of evidence from neuroscience, environmental psychology, physiology and architectural research, rather than through a systematic review or statistical modelling.

text.text: A domain was included where a class of environmental characteristics had repeatedly been associated with outcomes relevant to mental health, where a plausible neurobiological system mediating that association could be identified, and where the relevant characteristics could, at least in principle, be measured and modified through design.

The framework is intended to complement dimensional systems such as the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC), 67 which organise mental functioning into negative and positive valence systems, cognitive systems, systems for social processes, arousal and regulatory systems, and sensorimotor systems.
text.formatted: The framework is intended to complement dimensional systems such as the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC), <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67</ref> which organise mental functioning into negative and positive valence systems, cognitive systems, systems for social processes, arousal and regulatory systems, and sensorimotor systems.

text.text: Whereas RDoC describes functional systems within the person, the present domains describe classes of environmental characteristics and the person-environment interactions through which they engage those systems.

The two can therefore be mapped onto one another: Safety and Accessibility relates primarily to negative valence systems (threat and uncertainty), Cognitive Load and Environmental Complexity to cognitive systems, Multisensory Integration to perceptual aspects of cognitive and sensorimotor systems, Emotional Valence to positive and negative valence systems, Social Connection to systems for social processes, and Naturalness and Biophilia to arousal and regulatory systems relevant to stress recovery and restoration.
This correspondence suggests how environmental characteristics might be linked to transdiagnostic mechanisms, although it remains a conceptual proposal to be tested empirically.

The framework is conceptually informed by environmental enrichment research, largely from animal models, showing that complex, multisensory and socially stimulating environments can influence neuroplasticity, neurogenesis and behaviour. [68] [69] [70] Animal models provide a stronger basis for causal inference than most human studies, because environmental conditions can be randomly assigned and varied in isolation while genetic background is held constant.

text.text: In rodents, housing in enriched environments that combine physical complexity, novelty, social contact and opportunities for exploration increases adult hippocampal neurogenesis, improves learning and memory, and can reduce the impact of stress and of genetic risk in models of brain disorders. 68, 69 Translation to humans is nonetheless limited: enrichment is usually contrasted with impoverished standard laboratory housing, a contrast with no direct equivalent in human settings, and timescales, species-typical needs and social contexts differ substantially.

text.text: Animal work is therefore best treated as a source of mechanistic hypotheses, for example concerning hippocampal plasticity or stress-axis regulation, to be tested in human studies of specific environmental features.

The table presents a conceptual synthesis of converging evidence from neuroscience, environmental psychology, and built environment research.
The domains represent distinct yet interconnected dimensions of environmental experience and may therefore overlap to some extent.
The neural systems listed are likewise best understood as distributed and interacting networks principally associated with each domain, rather than as discrete one-to-one region-to-domain mappings.
The first domain covers environmental safety and spatial affordance, including how the physical environment supports a sense of safety, legibility, and wayfinding.
Neural systems such as the amygdala, hippocampus, and retrosplenial cortex underlie spatial orientation, vigilance, and environmental predictability.

Feeling safe is foundational to mental wellbeing and closely linked to stress management and comfort. 71 However, perceived safety is shaped not only by spatial form but also by broader individual, social, and contextual factors, including socioeconomic conditions, characteristics of the social environment, and gender-related differences in experiences of urban space. 72 Accessibility, particularly across physical and neurodiverse populations, is essential for inclusivity and autonomy, shaping how individuals perceive control and experience a space. 73, 74 Environments that provide clear sight lines, coherent spatial layouts, and balanced lighting may foster predictability, perceived safety, and ease of wayfinding, thereby reducing cognitive demand and potentially attenuating stress-related responses. text.text: The cognitive domain explores how environmental structure and complexity shape attention, creativity, and cognitive restoration.

The coupling of fronto-parietal control and default-mode networks has been argued to enable transitions between focus and reflection. 78 Stimulating yet coherent environments support curiosity and cognitive resilience. 79, 80 Spatial variety and structured complexity have the potential to encourage fascination without overload, supporting mental restoration and creativity. 81 Evidence relevant to this domain is convergent but methodologically heterogeneous, and further work is needed to clarify how an optimal level of complexity can be distinguished from overstimulation in real-world environments.

text.text: Human experience is inherently multisensory.
This domain examines how coherence across sensory channels (sight, sound, touch and temperature) affects comfort and predictability.

Neural integration across the thalamus, insula, and sensory cortices creates unified perceptual experiences. 65 Although multisensory coherence is likely to be important for comfort and stress regulation, the built-environment literature remains relatively fragmented, and more precise operationalisation of cross-modal effects is still needed. 61

text.text: The emotional domain captures how aesthetic and atmospheric qualities of the built environment influence affective states.

Neural systems including the orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and limbic structures underpin aesthetic pleasure, harmony, and mood regulation. 82 Environments that evoke positive emotions can buffer stress and support mental wellbeing. 83 Studies have reported associations between scenic locations, happiness, and wellbeing, 84, 85 suggesting that aesthetics should not be overlooked. 64 This domain should therefore be regarded as a plausible translational synthesis rather than a fully validated category, given that aesthetic appraisal reflects both shared neurobiological processes and substantial individual and cultural variation.

text.text: The social domain examines how architectural spaces can enable or constrain social interaction, togetherness, trust, and belonging, 86, 87 while recognising that spatial design shapes the opportunities for such outcomes rather than determining them, as trust, inclusion, discrimination, social capital, and broader institutional conditions remain decisive.

text.text: Neural systems including the medial prefrontal cortex and temporo-parietal junction are central to social cognition and empathy, while affiliative and bonding processes have also been linked to oxytocinergic mechanisms, whereby oxytocin released during positive social contact promotes trust and approach behaviour and dampens amygdala-mediated stress and threat responses, thereby reinforcing social bonds. 87, 88 The relationship between spatial form and social connection is also likely to be context-dependent, shaped not only by design features but by population characteristics, cultural norms, and wider social conditions.

text.text: The final domain addresses the human affinity for natural environments and their restorative impact on physiology and mood.

Activation of visual and default-mode networks, together with parasympathetic pathways, contributes to stress reduction, fascination, and recovery. 89 Exposure to vegetation, daylight, and water elements re-establishes sensory balance and fosters cognitive restoration. 7, 10 Being in nature and even in immersive virtual reality nature environments reduces subjective perception of stress, reduces cortisol, and improves heart rate variability (HRV). [90] [91] [92] Although this is one of the more consistent areas of the literature, important questions remain regarding which qualities of nature exposure are most relevant and through which pathways restorative effects are most likely to arise. 61

text.text: While each domain represents a distinct dimension of neuro-environmental interaction, they are interdependent and mutually reinforcing.
At present, however, the framework should be understood primarily as a translational and hypothesis-generating model, rather than as a fully validated empirical taxonomy for real-world application.

A future integrative account of built-environment effects will require nonlinear, multimodal and multilevel approaches that move beyond isolated exposure-outcome associations. 7, 93 Urban conditions emerge from interacting physical, social and biological processes whose effects may be synergistic, threshold-dependent and heterogeneous across individuals and contexts.

text.text: Computational frameworks should therefore combine environmental measures with neuroimaging, cognition, behaviour, whole-body physiology and multi-omics, and exposome, while accounting for temporal dynamics and individual trajectories. 7 Methods for evaluating the impact of urban environments linked to brain health Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides high-resolution measures of brain structure and function and has been central to research linking urban exposure to the brain. 8, 22 MRI has been used to examine structural and functional differences in stress-sensitive regions such as the amygdala, hippocampus and prefrontal cortex in relation to urban and environmental exposure. 12, 22 The principal limitation of conventional MRI in this field is ecological: scanning takes place in a controlled laboratory environment, while environmental exposure is usually inferred from separate geocoded, behavioural or self-report data.

text.text: Physiological markers provide a complementary and more portable window onto stress-related processes.

Cortisol, an index of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-axis activity, can be measured in saliva, blood or hair and is widely used as a marker of physiological stress. 94 It is relevant to environmental research because chronic stress is implicated in many mental health conditions, urban upbringing has been associated with altered stress processing, and sustained cortisol elevation has been linked to structural changes in stress-sensitive brain regions. 8, 95 Heart rate variability (HRV) indexes autonomic function through variation in inter-beat intervals and is inversely associated with sympathetic activation. 96 Higher HRV is generally associated with greater stress resilience and better mental health, whereas lower HRV has been linked to anxiety, depression and stress vulnerability. 97, 98 Wearable and mobile technologies increasingly allow neural and physiological responses to be studied in everyday settings.

text.text: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) measures electrical activity at the scalp and can track moment-to-moment neural dynamics as individuals move through real-world environments.

It offers high temporal resolution and greater ecological validity than laboratory-based neuroimaging, but has limited spatial resolution and is sensitive to movement and muscular artefacts. 99, 100 Although difficult to achieve in practice, the strongest designs will combine these approaches (Fig. 2).

text.text: Geospatial and longitudinal data can characterise the distribution and accumulation of environmental exposure; ecological momentary assessment and behavioural measures can capture subjective and functional responses; wearable physiology and mobile neurotechnology can track processes as they unfold; and MRI can provide spatially specific measures of brain structure and function.
Operationalising the domains also requires instruments that record environmental experience in a structured and comparable way.

One such approach applies the six domains described here as a domain-referenced self-report measure combined with structured environmental profiling, allowing overall and domain-specific scores to be compared across settings and before and after environmental change.
Three conclusions emerge from the evidence considered in this article.
First, the evidence remains predominantly associative.

Epidemiological, environmental and neuroimaging studies link urbanicity, limited exposure to natural environments and particular spatial conditions with psychiatric, cognitive and neurobiological outcomes.

However, causal interpretation is constrained by residential self-selection, migration, reverse causation, exposure misclassification, and the frequent use of broad environmental indicators or registry-based diagnoses.
The evidence therefore shows more clearly that environmental conditions are relevant to mental health than how particular spatial features produce specific outcomes.
Second, environmental exposures are correlated, interacting and cumulative.
Urban environments comprise overlapping conditions, including noise, air pollution, density, housing quality, traffic, daylight, deprivation, social context and access to natural environments.
Associations with individual features, including greenspace, must therefore be interpreted within the wider environmental and social exposure profile.
Third, the six-domain framework provides an integrative, hypothesis-generating structure for advancing the field beyond broad measures of urbanicity.
Prospective work should test the separability and interactions of these domains and establish their reliability and validity across populations and settings.
An important challenge is to bridge aggregate environmental indicators, subjective experience, biological embedding and mental health outcomes.

Existing studies have established associations between urbanisation, greenspace exposure, brain-related outcomes and mental health diagnoses, 5, 12, 21, 22 but a major gap remains in linking specific spatial qualities to particular neurobiological and psychological responses.

text.text: The evidence also remains heavily weighted towards the Global North, limiting generalisability to informal settlements and rapidly urbanising regions (e.g. sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia).
Developmentally informed studies, particularly in childhood and adolescence, will be important for determining when environmental exposure matters most and how effects accumulate across the lifespan.
Mechanistic randomised controlled trials are a particular priority.

These could test whether modifying features such as daylight, noise, access to nature, sensory conditions or spatial configuration alters hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-axis activity, autonomic regulation, affective responses or cognitive functioning.

If built environments contribute to mental health risk and resilience, environmental design may represent a scalable and non-stigmatising target for intervention across healthcare, education, workplaces, housing and public space.
Translational recommendations should, however, remain proportionate to the strength of the evidence.
The next step is to identify testable environmental features and mechanisms through rigorous longitudinal, experimental and real-world research.

With greater conceptual precision, methodological integration and empirical validation, environmental neuroscience may help inform built environments that are more responsive to the conditions supporting human wellbeing, resilience and mental health.

Fig 1 | Environmental pathways to mental health. a, Co-occurring built-environment conditions may influence mental health trajectories through environmental qualities and neurobiological and psychological responses, with effects accumulating over time.
These pathways may be moderated by developmental timing, sociocultural context, biological susceptibility, prior experience and adaptive capacity.

Feedback loops may arise when behavioural choices alter subsequent environmental exposure. b, Proposed neurobiological framework linking the external environment to mental health and brain-relevant functioning.

Six interrelated environmental quality domains: Safety and Accessibility, Cognitive Load and Environmental Complexity, Multisensory Integration, Emotional Valence, Social Connection, and Naturalness and Biophilia.
These domains provide a structure for examining relationships with perception and cognition, emotion, social processes, stress physiology, and broader neural and physiological functioning.
Cross-cutting socioeconomic, cultural and individual factors may further shape these relationships.

Fig 2 | Multimethod empirical approaches for studying links between built environments, brain-relevant functioning and mental health. a, Environmental exposures and human responses can be assessed across complementary real-world and laboratory settings.

Field-based measures can characterise features of urban and indoor environments, while ecological momentary assessment (EMA), geolocation, behavioural measures, wearable physiology, mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) can capture individual responses during everyday experience.

Laboratory and clinical approaches, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cognitive assessment and mental-health measures, provide complementary information at different spatial and temporal scales. b, Integrating environmental exposure measures with subjective experience, neural and physiological responses, behaviour and mental-health outcomes can help test candidate pathways linking environmental conditions to mental health.

Longitudinal, experimental, naturalistic and multilevel designs can further distinguish short-term responses from longer-term trajectories and strengthen inference about potential mechanisms and intervention targets.
